name: Skou
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 2 other works consulted do not discuss stress; 1 further work by the same author (or citing it for stress) agrees.

tone_statements.citation: Voorhoeve, C. L. 1971. Miscellaneous notes on languages in West Irian, New Guinea. In T. Dutton, C. Voorhoeve and S. A. Wurm (eds), Papers in New Guinea Linguistics No. 14 (Pacific Linguistics A-28), 47-114. Canberra: The Australian National University. [sec. 2.2 'The Sko language', pp. 54-59]
tone_statements.quote: There seem to be three tones in Sko. Cowan defined the tones as high, mid, and low. The writer's informant volunteered examples of three different tones, using monosyllabic words consisting of a consonant plus vowel. In citation forms the tones are realized as two falling and one rising tone, one falling tone having a slightly higher pitch than the other. [...] In a frame, the tones are realized as low, high, and low-high [...] In the monosyllabic words recorded, falling and rising tones are easily distinguished but further study would be needed to determine which falling tones are to be interpreted as low and which as high.
tone_statements.check: quotation verified in source (minor differences in wording)
tone_statements.n_tones: 3 (citation: two falling + one rising; in frame: low, high, low-high)

audit.action: a better source should be cited for the same classification
audit.reasoning: The classification (fixed-dominant, initial: root-initial stress with proclitics outside the domain, non-strict) rests on the fieldworker's full reference grammar, and the deciding quotation is verbatim at the cited section (locator should be tightened to p. 82, p. 118). The source PDF was not yet obtained before this compilation; it is now obtained by the project together with the 2007 revised draft, which repeats the section unchanged, so the blank strength of the evidence can be raised to primary-grammar/quote-verified. No better or competing description of Skou stress exists (the tone paper and acoustic appendix are silent on stress; no instrumental stress study found). One caution worth carrying in the record: Donohue states stress is phonetically weak (slight vowel lengthening) and easily masked by lexical tone in this tone language, so 'initial stress' is a low-salience property, not a robust accentual system. sources.citation: Donohue, Mark. 2004. A grammar of the Skou language of New Guinea. Ms. dated 3 October 2004, National University of Singapore. MPG PuRe item_402710 (823 pp PDF).
sources.quote: 'In a monomorphemic word stress is on the initial syllable ... On these words stress is realised as a slight lengthening of the vowel in the stressed syllable. Stress is thus completely predictable, and is assigned to the first syllable in a simple word. In a word with proclitics, we find that stress remains on the first syllable of the root ... Under reduplication stress remains with the original root, and not with the reduplicant. ... with a suffix such as the applicative -na we similarly find no change in the position of the stress. ... the perceptual and acoustic correlates of stress are n

sources.citation: Donohue, Mark. 2006. Skou Languages. In Keith Brown (ed.), Encyclopedia of Language & Linguistics, 2nd edition, vol. 11, 402-403. Oxford: Elsevier. doi:10.1016/B0-08-044854-2/04599-5
sources.note: Describes another variety (Glottolog skoo1245). Family-level statement (Skou family, 16 languages incl. Skou of the Skou villages east of Humboldt Bay): tone features prominently in all the languages; tonal contrasts range from three to six on a monosyllabic word, and in all well-investigated cases (Skou being the best-investigated) the domain of tone is the morpheme, not the syllable. No Skou-specific tone inventory is given; cross-refers to Donohue 2003c 'The tonal system of Skou' and Cowan 1952 'Een toon-taal'.
